scores.evidence: Agent PRs trigger CI through `pull_request`, never `pull_request_target`.
scores.rationale: Technical claims are precise, including subtle ones (webhook 10s timeout, HMAC, SKIP LOCKED, pull_request_target), but the Phase 1 'Contents read' scope is insufficient for Phase 5 branch pushes, contradicting the plan's own re-approval rationale.

scores.evidence: triages new issues (labels, duplicates, owner, missing-info requests) and, when a maintainer opts in, attempts a fix that it opens as a draft PR
scores.rationale: Covers triage and resolution exactly as asked, resolves ambiguities with sensible opt-in defaults, and every exclusion is explicit with a pull-forward trigger.

scores.evidence: The orchestrator, which is outside the sandbox, is the only thing holding write credentials.
scores.rationale: Responsibilities, data ownership and trust boundaries are consistent everywhere, with cross-cutting concerns (identity, idempotency, auditing) applied uniformly per phase without contradictions.

scores.evidence: agreement on the top label is at least 85% on the held-out set (a starting target, recalibrated after measuring how often maintainers agree
scores.rationale: Every phase has a checkable exit criterion tied to a specific risk (red-team suite, escape suite, shadow mode, hidden-test replay), targets are labeled provisional, and validation continues post-launch.

scores.evidence: Revisit trigger | We need a multi-region deployment (more than one region writing at once) for an SLA.
scores.rationale: Key decisions are stated as defaults with explicit conditions that would change them, numbers are framed as budgets or starting targets, and no unsupported certainty is asserted.

scores.evidence: Someone puts a prompt injection in an issue body and the agent leaks secrets or lands malicious code, for example by editing a CI workflow
scores.rationale: The hardest domain failures — injection, CI-workflow exfiltration, webhook duplicates, poison events, sandbox escape, runaway loops, feedback poisoning, crash recovery — each get concrete detection and containment.

scores.evidence: Alerts fire on job failure rate above 5% or queue age above 5 min.
scores.rationale: Day-zero deployment, tracing, meaningful alerts, kill switch and prompt rollback are concrete and team-sized, but incident ownership and code-deploy rollback are not explicitly addressed.

scores.evidence: Triage: at most 8k input tokens, $0.05 and 60 s. Resolution: at most $3, 20 min and 40 tool calls.
scores.rationale: The dominant inference cost is capped per task, repo and globally with routing to cheap models and a cost-based self-host trigger, but overall run-cost estimates and engineering-time costs are absent.

scores.evidence: Changing this later means asking every installation to re-approve, so it goes first.
scores.rationale: Hard-to-reverse choices (App permissions, event schema versioning, provider abstraction) get early scrutiny and isolation, while reversible choices (Postgres queue, no broker) are made quickly with explicit revisit triggers.

scores.evidence: Modular monolith (webhook ingest, orchestrator and worker in one deployable) plus one forced boundary: the sandbox runner
scores.rationale: Starts with the simplest workable design, justifies the one extra boundary on security grounds, and defers multi-agent, brokers and dashboards behind concrete triggers without omitting essentials.

scores.evidence: Exit check: a real issue on the sandbox repo gets a real comment in production, and its end-to-end trace plus the token and cost metric
scores.rationale: A team could start immediately: Phase 0 is a concrete slice, ordering is justified by dependencies, each phase has verifiable exit checks, and adaptation triggers are specified.

checklist.evidence: Runs without approval: reading, retrieval, sandbox runs... Requires approval: starting a resolution, opening a PR... Never allowed: merging, pushing to the default branch, editing workflows.
Grant least privilege: Issues read/write, Contents read, Pull requests write, Metadata read. Do not grant Workflows or Administration.
Issue text, comments, repo files, tool output and test logs are all treated as untrusted data.
Each job gets a new gVisor or Firecracker microVM, destroyed after the job. There's no GitHub token and no cloud credentials inside it.
on a replay set of 50 or more past closed issues (held out, with the real fix's tests as hidden tests)
Build 200 or more historical issues per pilot repo, with labels set by maintainers, as a frozen, versioned held-out set.
Record PR merged, merged after edits, or closed, plus label corrections by maintainers and 👍/👎 reactions on agent comments
A global kill switch (a config flag checked before every external write) exists from the start.
Hard caps on tokens, cost, wall-clock time and tool calls for each job, plus a daily cap per repo and a global circuit breaker.
The `action_log` table is append-only and records who, what, why, the model version, the prompt hash and the approval reference.
For code, use search inside the sandbox (ripgrep plus a symbol index) instead of embedding the whole repo.
give every outbound write an idempotency key, and re-read issue state before writing (skip if the issue is closed, locked or already labeled by a human)

traps.evidence: The agent never merges and never pushes to the default branch. Resolution ends at a draft PR on `agent/issue-<n>`.
There's no GitHub token and no cloud credentials inside it.
Issue bodies, comments, repo files and test logs are all treated as data and placed in the user turn inside delimiters
at least 30% produce PRs that pass the hidden tests, with zero diff-policy violations
a synthetic loop is cut off at 40 calls and emits `budget_exceeded{repo,class}`.

note: An exceptionally strong plan that avoids every trap and concretely covers nearly the whole domain checklist; the only notable gaps are the Contents-read permission inconsistency, no explicit reproduce-before-fix step, and thin incident-ownership and total-cost estimates.
